overview:
Organisation of Classical Languages K–10

The diagram (Figure 1) is an overview of the Classical Languages K–10 Syllabus. It shows that:

  • understanding texts is necessary to access classical languages and cultures. Students apply knowledge of language systems to understand texts
  • translation is a core skill in the study of a classical language. By translating texts, the analysis of language reinforces meaning
  • intercultural understanding involves learning about the classical world, making connections and comparisons, and reflecting on language, culture and identity.

Across a stage of learning all focus areas need to be taught.

Below the first focus area is 'Understanding and responding', 'Applying knowledge of language systems' and 'Translating'. Below the second focus area is 'Understanding the world of the target language' and 'Reflecting on language, culture and identity'.

Creating written texts supports learning

The development of the Classical Languages Syllabus follows Recommendation 2: ‘Clarify and strengthen writing content in syllabus documents’ from Teaching Writing: Report of the Thematic Review of Writing (NESA 2018).

Creating written texts facilitates learning as it promotes explicitness, encourages the integration of ideas, supports reflection, fosters personal engagement and aids learners to think about the significance and implication of ideas. Each subject has particular and specific writing demands relevant for communicating within and about the discipline. Writing about content enhances understanding across subjects and stages.

The secondary curriculum includes:

  • systematic development of expectations for creating written texts which align with the English K–10 Syllabus (2022)
  • explicit writing content to support students to become fluent creators of texts and to deepen their understanding of the subject area
  • opportunities to practise the process of creating written texts to develop and communicate knowledge, understanding and ideas
  • a focus on development of word consciousness and precise use of subject-specific terminology.

Creating written texts refers to the act of composing and constructing a text for a particular purpose, audience and context.

Various methods of transcription may be employed, and a student’s preferred communication form(s) should be considered when teaching.

Balance of content

Syllabus framework

The Classical Languages K–10 Syllabus is a framework that can be used to teach a classical language in New South Wales. A classical language is any language with an independent literary tradition and a large and ancient body of written literature. Classical Languages are no longer spoken as a first language.

overviewSections.heading: Access content points
overviewSections.html:
Access content points have been developed to support students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards Early Stage 1 outcomes. These students may communicate using verbal and/or nonverbal forms.

For each of the Early Stage 1 outcomes, access content points are provided to indicate content that students with significant intellectual disability may access as they work towards the outcomes. Teachers will use the access content points on their own, or in combination with the content for each outcome. 

Decisions regarding curriculum options for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

overviewSections.heading: Life Skills outcomes and content
overviewSections.html:
Students with disability can access the syllabus outcomes and content in a range of ways. Decisions regarding curriculum options should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Some students with intellectual disability may find the Years 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content the most appropriate option to follow in Stage 4 and/or Stage 5. Before determining whether a student is eligible to undertake a course based on Life Skills outcomes and content, consideration should be given to other ways of assisting the student to engage with the Stage 4 and/or Stage 5 outcomes, or prior stage outcomes if appropriate. This assistance may include a range of adjustments to teaching, learning and assessment activities.

Life Skills outcomes cannot be taught in combination with other outcomes from the same subject. Teachers select specific Life Skills outcomes to teach based on the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of each student. Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Life Skills outcomes.

overviewSections.heading: Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities
overviewSections.html:
NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

overviewSections.heading: Balance of content
overviewSections.html:
The amount of content associated with a given outcome is not necessarily indicative of the amount of time spent engaging with the respective outcome. Teachers use formative and summative assessment to determine instructional priorities and the time needed for students to demonstrate expected outcomes.

In considering the intended learning, teachers make decisions about the sequence and emphasis to be given to particular groups of content based on the needs and abilities of their students.

overviewSections.heading: Syllabus framework
overviewSections.html: The Classical Languages K–10 Syllabus is a framework that can be used to teach a classical language in New South Wales. A classical language is any language with an independent literary tradition and a large and ancient body of written literature. Classical Languages are no longer spoken as a first language.

rationale:
Through the study of a Classical language and its texts, students immerse themselves in ancient worlds that have shaped the thought, languages, literatures, cultures and traditions of contemporary societies.

Learning a Classical language positions students to consider multiple ways of thinking and being. Students are exposed to new ways of viewing the world by accessing texts that give insight into ancient perspectives and lifestyles. Through texts, students examine social, ethical and political value systems and their impact.

Investigating Classical societies encourages students to be open to the perspectives of others. Students expand their understanding of the world to include the diversity of languages and cultures that have continued to be an integral feature of society since ancient times. They learn about and engage with these languages and cultures in ways that recognise commonalities and differences and create connections. This challenges them to reflect on their own identity, values, attitudes, beliefs and citizenship.

The study of a Classical language, translation and the movement between language systems promote mental agility and the development of literacy skills. Students broaden their vocabulary and metalanguage, gain an understanding of how languages work and learn to become better communicators. The nature of Classical languages requires students to pay close attention to detail, applying their critical and creative thinking, and exercising memory. As students engage with rich Classical texts and the literary traditions of the target language culture, they consider the use of language to present events and ideas, and learn to interpret meaning. All these skills support students in other learning areas, including learning additional languages.

Through studying a Classical language students acquire transferable skills for life, expand and enrich their perspective on the world and become engaged global citizens.
aim:
The aim of Classical Languages K–10 is to empower students with the knowledge, understanding and skills required to access and appreciate a range of Classical texts.

Students:

  • develop linguistic competence in the target language
  • develop their understanding of how language is used to communicate meaning
  • develop their understanding of the impact of Classical civilisations on the contemporary world
  • reflect on their own and others’ languages, cultures and identity
  • develop an interest in and enjoyment of language learning.

items.text: Reflect on the interrelationship between languages and on how identity is shaped by languages, cultures, attitudes, values and beliefs
items.examples:
Discuss how learning the target language and culture may affect students’ values and attitudes, their response to multiple perspectives and ideas, and understanding of their own heritage, language and culture.

Reflect on the role of language in preserving cultural identity by researching endangered languages and issues of language reclamation and maintenance, including Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Languages.

outcomes.description: responds to a range of texts to demonstrate understanding
participates in the translation of modelled vocabulary, phrases or texts into English

contentGroups.title: Understanding and responding to target language texts

items.text: Recognise familiar vocabulary in the target language
items.examples:
Recognise greetings in the target language.

Identify words, phrases and simple sentences.

items.text: Sequence key vocabulary and phrases in the target language
items.examples:
Order words to form a simple phrase, a greeting or familiar classroom instruction.

Match words or phrases to characters in a story.

items.text: Identify main ideas in texts
items.examples:
Use gestures, actions, images, words or Aboriginal hand talk/hand signs to describe the main idea of a song, rhyme or story.

Identify names of characters, places and other key vocabulary in songs, rhymes or stories.

items.text: Respond to known vocabulary or phrases in the target language
items.examples:
Create an image to represent a familiar word.

Match familiar vocabulary with photographs or pictures.

Identify familiar vocabulary in a text to get the gist of the text.

items.text: Respond to texts in familiar contexts
items.examples:
Participate in sequencing pictures and phrases to order events in a story.

Participate in creating descriptive sentences about people or places in a text.

Use word banks or images to interpret a text.

contentGroups.title: Applying knowledge of the language system and text features to understand, interpret and respond to target language texts

items.text: Recognise the sounds of the target language
items.examples:
Match pronunciations with words in the target language.

Engage in songs, chants or performance to develop pronunciation, phrasing and intonation.

Engage in a dramatic reading or recitation of a text.

items.text: Respond to the language system or structure of a text
items.examples:
Recognise word order patterns in known language structures.

Use the structure of a text to identify the purpose and audience.

items.text: Apply knowledge of vocabulary or text features to understand texts
items.examples:
Recognise familiar vocabulary in a text.

Use text features to answer who, what, when, where or why questions about a text.

items.text: Recognise key vocabulary in the target language writing system
items.examples:
Recognise words written in the target language writing system.

Match words or pictures with words written in the target language writing system.

items.text: Engage in writing vocabulary using the target language writing system
items.examples:
Trace or copy symbols to form words using the target language writing system.

Use modelling clay or trace in sand or salt to form words using the target language writing system.

contentGroups.title: Translating target language texts

items.text: Recognise and translate key vocabulary or phrases in familiar contexts into English
items.examples:
Label familiar people or places in the target language.

Participate in creating a bilingual word wall of everyday words in English and in the target language.

items.text: Translate simple texts in familiar contexts into English
items.examples:
Repeat a modelled translation of words from the target language into English.

Access vocabulary using charts, tables or word lists to translate a text into English.

Participate in translating key information in familiar contexts into English.

items.text: Translate texts into English, applying knowledge of language systems, text features or culture
items.examples:
Use scaffolds to translate a text independently or collaboratively.

Use knowledge of cultural practices to participate in translating a short, spoken text in a familiar context.

outcomes.description: recognises connections between contemporary and target languages, culture(s) or identity

contentGroups.title: Understanding the world of the target language

items.text: Demonstrate awareness of linguistic and cultural diversity
items.examples:
Engage in discussions about the diverse cultural backgrounds of peers and the languages spoken at home through gestures, images, spoken language, writing or Aboriginal Sign Languages.

Locate country(ies) of origin for the target language on a map or globe.

items.text: Engage with practices of the target language culture
items.examples:
Research celebrations to learn about the beliefs, traditions and values of the target language culture.

Engage in a cultural celebration, practice or historical re-enactment.

Identify features of the target language culture, such as food, music or celebrations.

items.text: Explore the target language culture through texts
items.examples:
Recognise visual representations of the target language culture.

Explore the target language culture through songs, poems or stories and communicate ideas using gestures, images, spoken language, writing or Aboriginal Sign Languages.

contentGroups.title: Reflecting on language, culture and identity

items.text: Explore similarities and differences between cultures
items.examples:
Participate in discussions about the similarities or differences between the lives of people today and those of the target language culture, through gestures, images, spoken language or writing.

Compare celebrations in cultures, including those of the target language culture, and communicate ideas using gestures, images, spoken language, writing or Aboriginal Sign Languages.

items.text: Identify how language, culture and identity are connected
items.examples:
Identify features of the lifestyle of the target language culture, such as family structure and roles, festivals and celebrations.

Identify connections between target language culture and Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Cultures and Peoples, such as similarities in food, clothing, story or trading connections.

Participate in discussions about the influence of the target language culture on language, culture and identity today through gestures, images, spoken language or writing.

outcomes.description: analyses and responds to information to demonstrate understanding of a range of moderately complex texts
translates a range of moderately complex texts into English

contentGroups.title: Understanding and responding to target language texts

items.text: Interpret information, purpose and perspective in a range of synthetic and/or original texts, seen and unseen
items.examples: Interpret and compare purpose and perspective across different text types such as historical narratives, myths, speeches, epic poetry and epigrams.

items.text: Recognise different layers of meaning
items.examples: Such as fact and opinion, stated and implied meaning, literal and figurative meaning.

items.text: Identify cohesive devices to track meaning across different parts of a moderately complex text
items.examples: Recognise the function of connectives, conjunctions and discourse markers in moderately complex texts to determine the relationship between sentences and ideas and to support comprehension.

items.text: Select appropriate resources to support the comprehension and interpretation of texts
Respond to a range of texts critically and creatively in the target language or in English
items.examples:
Respond to analysis questions on texts and identify specific examples of linguistic, text and/or literary features, explaining their effect.

Write a reflection on a text from the perspective of a character from the story or another individual from the target language culture.

contentGroups.title: Applying knowledge of language systems and text features to understand, interpret and respond to target language texts

items.text: Use knowledge of a range of grammar structures in simple, compound and complex sentences
items.examples:
Understand the role of mood, voice and subordinate clauses in determining meaning.

Translate sentences or continuous texts into the target language to consolidate understanding of grammar.

items.text: Use knowledge of a wide range of vocabulary
Use knowledge of culture, and linguistic, literary and text features
items.examples:
Cultural knowledge such as the cultural and historical context of a text, author or genre.

Literary features such as simile, metaphor, hyperbole, juxtaposition, personification, anaphora and irony, and how they contribute to stylistic effectiveness.

items.text: Use a range of metalanguage to describe grammatical, literary and text features
Use pronunciation, intonation and phrasing to demonstrate understanding of the text's meaning and purpose
items.examples: Recite or perform plays, speeches and poetry, adapting the delivery to suit the genre, with consideration of metre and rhythm where appropriate.

items.text: Use knowledge of a range of sound–symbol correspondences and features of the target language writing system

contentGroups.title: Translating target language texts

items.text: Produce coherent and comprehensible English translations of a range of synthetic and/or original texts
items.examples:
Analyse complex sentence structures in the target language text and determine appropriate English equivalents.

Recognise that complex sentences in the target language may need to be translated into more than one sentence in English and that punctuation may have to be adjusted to ensure fluency.

items.text: Produce translations that retain the emphasis, tone and register of the original text and reflect the author's purpose
items.examples: Analyse the background, text type, tone and language of the original text before attempting a translation.

items.text: Compare different translations of the same text to identify features of successful translations
items.examples: Evaluate the effectiveness of translations using vocabulary, grammatical accuracy, fluency, clarity, idiomatic expression and reflection of the author’s intent as criteria.
